senses.gloss:
dhvajastambha
(‘flagpost’)
------------------------------------------
One of the essential parts of a traditional Hindu temple is the ध्वज-stambha or the flagpost. The actual temple, in the ritualistic sense extends from the garbhamandira (sanctum) up to the ध्वजस्तम्भ.
Since a temple is considered as the ‘palace’ of God, the emperor of emperors, it must have a flagpost in front of it, in a prominent place. The lāñchana or insignia, made of copper or brass and fixed like a flag to the top of the post, varies according to the deity in the temple. The figure on the lāñchana is invariably that of the वाहन (the mount) of the deity. For instance, in शिव temples it contains नन्दि; in देवी temples, the lion; in विष्णु temples, गरुड and so on.

dhvani
(‘sound’)
------------------------------------------
The word ‘dhvani’ means ‘sound’. It may be buddhihetuka (caused by the intellect) or abuddhihetuka (not caused by the intellect). The sound of thunder is an example for the latter.
Buddhihetuka sounds, again, can be svābhāvika (natural), like the sound of weeping or laughter. Or, it can be kālpanika (produced by imagination) like speaking or मुसिच्.
In the Alaṅkāraśāstra (the science of figure of speech) ‘dhvani’ means suggested meaning, such usage being generally found in poetical works. Going into intricate details, the works on अलङ्कार list as many as 5355 varieties of ध्वनि!
See also SPHOṬAVĀDA.

dhvaja
(‘that [which] stands tall;’ a flag fixed on a post.)
------------------------------------------
A flag or a banner called ‘dhvaja’ fixed on a post is a common feature in हिन्दु तेम्प्लेस्. The post is called ‘dhvaja-stambha’ and the flag itself is a metallic plate, either of copper or of brass. It contains the figure of the वाहन (carrier mount) of the main deity in the temple. For instance, if it is a temple of शिव, the figure on the banner will be that of a bull (Nandi). If of देवी, it will be a lion. If of विष्णु, it will be गरुड (eagle-mount).
The dhvajas or flags made of cloth are hoisted in temples temporarily on special occasions like ब्रह्मोत्सव and रथोत्सव. (See BRAHMOTSAVA and RATHOTSAVA.)
The saṁnyāsins of some Hindu religious orders also carry a ध्वज on their staffs.

Dhvaja-Gaṇapati
(‘Gaṇapati with a banner’)
------------------------------------------
Gaṇapati or गणेश is an extremely popular deity of the Hindus and is worshiped at the start of all ventures, sacred or secular. Out of the 32 forms described in the iconographical works, ‘Dhvaja-गणपति’ (also called ‘Dvija-गणपति’) is one. He is depicted as a fierce deity of the colour of full-मोओन्, with four heads and four hands. In these four hands he is carrying a book, a rosary, a water pot and a flagstaff (daṇḍa with ध्वज). The name is probably derived from the last item.

dhvaṁsābhāva
(‘non-existence after destruction’)
------------------------------------------
This is the same as pradhvaṁsā-भाव. See ABHĀVA for details.
